problem: Existing World Action Models predict future video frames, which is expensive and only an indirect view of vehicle motion, and they ignore passive underwater dynamics (inertial glide, thruster dead band, currents, buoyancy/drag). VLA baselines imitate expert actions in 16-step chunks without evaluating outcomes, and they degrade when the DVL loses bottom lock.
motivation: An underwater vehicle keeps moving after a command ends, and centimeter-level grasping requires small commands that fall inside the thruster dead band. Predicting the physical state directly is more informative and much cheaper than predicting images, and it can run onboard embedded hardware. The same predictor can also stand in for a failed DVL.
key_idea: Replace video prediction with a compact learned predictor of the vehicle's 19/35-dimensional sensor-measured physical state, and choose thruster commands by scoring 128 imagined two-second rollouts (MPC-style), with cameras used only for goal and object-pose perception.
insight: Choosing actions by predicted outcome, rather than imitation, is what drives the gains. Removing imagination drops success from 72.6% to 31.9% (grasping 65.4% to 16.5%), and removing task-agnostic play drops it to 34.1%. Removing the disturbance token drops it to 43.6%. With the benchmark's object pose, predicted thrust pulses grasp in 85.2% of trials versus 17.9% for a hand-tuned law, so the gain comes from knowing where a pulse ends up rather than from cadence, closure trigger or grid size.
method: Physical-state predictor: a nominal MLP plus a residual MLP predict a 0.5 s state offset from the current state and the command chunk. Four chained calls give a 2 s horizon (H=20 steps of 0.1 s). The state is 19-dim (DVL, IMU, depth, last thrust) or 35-dim (adds joint encoders and object pose in the gripper frame). The model has 2.4M/2.6M parameters.
Disturbance token: a GRU encoder over the last 1.6 s of states and commands gives a 96-dim token capturing ambient current and thruster efficiency; it is trained jointly with the predictor.

Prediction-before-action planner: 128 structured candidates (thrust-allocation law over gains, hold, single-axis moves, play snippets) are rolled out in two rounds, the second around the 16 best. They are scored by a cost J on goal velocity, thrust, speed cap and spin, and the first 0.5 s of the winner is executed.

Thrust-pulse fine positioning: within 10 cm of the object, the candidates are discrete pulses (direction, magnitude 0.12–0.40, duration ≤0.4 s) followed by a coast. Each is scored on the predicted final gripper–object offset (weighted by Q with ±0.7 cm tolerance) and on residual velocity. A learned outcome head closes the gripper at p≥0.7.

Semantic perception heads: DINOv2-base heads convert the two camera images and the instruction into a waypoint displacement, the object pose and the box location. They are trained on demonstrations plus DAgger-style relabeled rollouts, and the predictor stays fixed.

DVL-loss estimator: the same network with the velocity channels masked, using three velocity heads whose mean is the estimate and whose spread gives sigma. A CUSUM-style trust statistic gates how far decisions may depart from the last DVL-based one. It can also act as a takeover layer for U0.

setting.backbone: Small MLP/GRU dynamics predictor (2.4M/2.6M) + DINOv2-base perception heads (86M each), trained from scratch/fine-tuned
setting.training_data: USIM demonstrations (20 tasks) plus task-agnostic play data (OU exploration, scene passes, deployment log); 3,488 recorded gripper closures for the outcome model; DAgger-relabeled rollouts for the perception heads
setting.observation: Two cameras plus DVL, IMU, pressure sensor and joint encoders; language instruction
setting.action_space: 13 low-level commands: 8 thruster values in [-1,1] plus 5 arm joint targets, in 0.1 s steps
setting.simulator: USIM benchmark on Stonefish (BlueROV2-class vehicle with arm)
setting.privileged: none (the 85.2% grasp analysis uses the benchmark's GT object pose, an analysis setting only). USIM's task schema supplies sub-goal ordering and goal velocity.

numbers.eval_set_note: 20 tasks, 700 trials (160 nav, 480 grasp, 40 transport, 20 track)
numbers.extra: trained on USIM demos plus play data; full sensing
numbers.evidence: Table 1 (Results on the 20 USIM tasks): AquaWAM 72.6% (508/700); U0 51.7%

numbers.eval_set_note: same 700 trials with DVL loss partway through every trial
numbers.backbone: AquaWAM predictor used as velocity estimator

numbers_note: USIM is not in the canonical benchmark list, so it is listed as other:USIM. Its split is not named; 'test' is used. Some success counts are as printed in the tables (e.g. Transport SSR 67.5% vs 3/40 for the DVL row looks inconsistent in the paper).
results: AquaWAM reaches 72.6% overall success on the 20 USIM tasks, versus 51.7% for the strongest baseline U0 and 39.4% for GR00T N1.5. It keeps 61.6% under DVL dropout against 39.4% for U0. It decides 2.7× faster than U0 on a Jetson AGX Orin (79.5 ms vs 214 ms per chunk), with a predictor of 2.4–2.6M parameters vs 2.7B for U0.
limitations: All results are in simulation; real-world sensor noise, latency and intermittent DVL dropouts are untested.
Transport after DVL loss remains at 7.5% (3/40), and a fully failed thruster (not seen in play) leaves only 4/40 gotos successful.

Perception is a bottleneck: 65.4% grasp success from the wrist camera versus 85.2% with the GT object pose. It also relies on USIM's task schema for sub-goal ordering, and under stricter judges it does not beat U0 at 0.25–0.5 m goto tolerances.
